title: Metric k-Median at the coverage-hardness threshold
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
formal: For every fixed rational \(\varepsilon>0\), does there exist one uniform randomized polynomial-bit-time algorithm that, on every metric k-Median instance defined below, always outputs a nonempty facility set \(S\subseteq F\) with \(|S|\le k\), and satisfies \[\Pr\!\left[\operatorname{cost}(S)\le\left(1+\frac2e+\varepsilon\right)\operatorname{OPT}\right]\ge\frac23?\] Here \(e=\exp(1)\). The polynomial and program may depend on fixed \(\varepsilon\), but the running time must be polynomial in the full input length on every execution, with unrestricted input \(k\).
definitions:
For the context, let \(\mathcal R\) be the set of fixed approximation factors achievable by the uniform randomized, always-feasible, worst-case polynomial-time algorithms below, with success probability at least \(2/3\) on each instance; let \(\rho_{\mathrm{med}}=\inf\mathcal R\). Write \(e=\exp(1)\). 

An input is \(I=(v,C,F,k,d)\), with \(v\ge1\), \(V=[v]=\{1,\ldots,v\}\), nonempty \(C,F\subseteq V\), \(C\cup F=V\), and an integer \(1\le k\le|F|\). The sets may overlap. The full table \(d:V\times V\to\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\) is promised to be a metric: \(d(x,y)=d(y,x)\), \(d(x,y)=0\) if and only if \(x=y\), and \(d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)\) for all points. There are no weights or capacities: each client in \(C\) has unit demand, and facilities must be chosen from the supplied \(F\).

For a nonempty \(S\subseteq F\), let \[\operatorname{cost}(S)=\sum_{c\in C}\min_{s\in S}d(c,s),\qquad \operatorname{OPT}=\min_{S\subseteq F,\ 1\le|S|\le k}\operatorname{cost}(S).\] Both minima are over finite nonempty sets. The output need only specify the selected facilities; no assignment or optimality certificate is required. Feasibility is mandatory even on random executions where the approximation inequality fails. No extra facilities are allowed in such executions or merely on average. Zero optimum is included: in that case the successful executions must have exactly zero cost. In a metric this case occurs precisely when \(C\subseteq F\) and \(|C|\le k\); a quotient by the optimum is never used in the definition.

Fix a concrete binary encoding. For a nonnegative integer \(t\), write \(u(t)=1^a0\operatorname{bin}(t+1)\), where \(\operatorname{bin}\) has no leading zeros and \(a\) is its length. The input concatenates \(u(v)\), \(u(k)\), the two \(v\)-bit membership masks for \(C,F\), and the \(v^2\) rational entries in row-major order. An entry is a reduced pair \(p/q\) with integers \(p\ge0,q\ge1\), encoded by \(u(p)u(q)\); zero uses \(p=0,q=1\). The total length of this entire string is \(L\). A facility set is output as a \(v\)-bit membership mask. No bound on numerators or denominators is assumed beyond their finite encoding.

The model is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program, a read-only input tape, initially blank work and output tapes, and ordinary charged tape transitions. A random transition reads one fresh independent fair bit. Running time counts every transition, including preprocessing, arithmetic, random-bit generation and output; the stated polynomial bound holds on every random execution. There is no advice depending on input length, oracle, quantum operation or unit-cost arbitrary-precision arithmetic. Behavior on strings outside the input promise is irrelevant. Success probability is over the random bits for each fixed input, not over an input distribution, and no single choice of coins must work for all inputs.

The factor \(r\) indexes an existence statement; it is not a real-valued input to the program. Different fixed factors may use different finite programs and polynomial constants. No computable rule converting an arbitrary real factor to a program is required. Both \(k\) and \(v\) vary within every such program’s input domain. Known constant-factor algorithms make \(\mathcal R\) nonempty, and \(\mathcal R\subseteq[1,\infty)\); hence its real infimum exists. The infimum need not be attained. No Euclidean, bounded-dimension, stability, sparsity or other additional promise is imposed.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed assertion or of its logical negation, with exactly the stated model, quantifier order and parameter dependence. A bound for a restricted subclass or one particular algorithm is insufficient to refute a universal existence assertion. Determining the entire optimal rate or a numerical approximation to it is not required.

progress.text: Feige proves the \(1- 1/e\) hardness threshold for Max k-Cover, which yields the \(1+2/e\) metric k-Median gap through a client–facility metric construction.
Jain–Mahdian–Saberi give the classical k-Median lower bound via Set Cover approximation; Theorem 10 states the historical reduction.
Cohen-Addad–Gupta–Kumar–Lee–Li reach \(1+2/e+\varepsilon\) in fixed-parameter time with respect to k, not unrestricted polynomial time.
Cohen-Addad–Grandoni–Lee–Schwiegelshohn–Svensson obtain a randomized polynomial-time \(2+\varepsilon\) approximation with at most k facilities; the May 2026 full-version revision retains the theorem.
Improved approximation-scheme runtimes apply to low-dimensional Euclidean clustering, a restricted metric setting.
Spectral dual fitting improves k-Means approximation; squared-distance clustering is a different objective.
Iterative randomized rounding yields another \((2+\varepsilon)\)-approximation with the true facility budget (Corollary 1.2); its intermediate expected-budget guarantee is distinct.

status_note: Checked through 16 September 2026. The source’s optimal general-metric approximation ratio remains undetermined in this bounded review. The May2026 full version retains a2+epsilon true-budget approximation; April2026 iterative rounding gives the same endpoint. Thus the infimum is at most2 unconditionally. context_blocks.text: The selected binary target is an algorithm for every factor \(1+2/e+\varepsilon\), where \(\varepsilon>0\) is fixed. This matches the familiar coverage-hardness scale from above without assuming that an algorithm attains the exact endpoint.

Metric k-Median chooses service locations and minimizes the sum of client travel distances. It also models selecting representatives for clustering. Clients and candidate facilities may be different sets, and the metric need not have Euclidean coordinates. The unresolved ratio measures how much optimization quality is lost when an arbitrary metric instance must be processed in polynomial time.

The known unconditional bounds give \(1\le\rho_{\mathrm{med}}\le2\). The upper endpoint follows from the \((2+\varepsilon)\)-approximation for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\); it does not assert a factor-two algorithm. Under \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{RP}\), the coverage hardness below gives \(\rho_{\mathrm{med}}\ge1+2/e\approx1.73576\). These are different kinds of bounds. In particular, \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\) would imply \(\rho_{\mathrm{med}}=1\).

Feige’s Theorem 5.3 gives an NP-hard coverage gap: all elements can be covered by \(k\) sets, or every such collection covers at most a \(1-1/e+\eta\) fraction, for any fixed \(\eta>0\). The associated client–facility metric uses separate copies of elements and sets, with cross distances one for incidence and three otherwise, and distance two between distinct points on the same side. Covering a fraction \(p\) corresponds to cost \((3-2p)|U|\), where \(U\) is the universe. Thus the gap becomes \(1\) versus \(1+2/e-2\eta\) per client.

This gap also explains the randomized assumption. A returned feasible solution of sufficiently small cost certifies the positive side; on a negative instance no such solution exists. Consequently a bounded-error algorithm beating the threshold would put the underlying NP-hard decision problem in \(\mathrm{RP}\), the class with polynomial time, one-sided error and no false acceptance. The exclusion for this card is therefore conditional on \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{RP}\), rather than justified by \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) alone.

Jain–Mahdian–Saberi’s 2002 Theorem 10 instead derives the classical k-Median lower bound from a Set Cover approximation barrier. The historical complexity assumption stated there is \(\mathrm{NP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{DTIME}(n^{O(\log\log n)})\). Feige’s ordinary NP-hardness theorem for Max k-Cover and its metric gap distinguish the stronger coverage-based conclusion from the assumption in that earlier Set Cover argument.

Theorem 1.1 of the STOC 2025 paper, retained in its May 2026 full revision, gives a randomized polynomial-time \((2+\varepsilon)\)-approximation with a feasible facility budget. The separate Theorem 1.2 allows extra centers, but this is not the budget of the final theorem. Lemma 1.4 relates bounded integer distances to general distances, so the result is not confined to a fixed distance precision.

Byrka and coauthors’ April 2026 paper supplies another \((2+\varepsilon)\)-approximation for metric k-Median, in Corollary 1.2. Its intermediate guarantee opens \(k\) facilities only in expectation; the final approximation restores the facility budget with an \(\varepsilon\) loss. This distinction matters: an expected budget permits some outcomes with too many facilities and does not meet the card’s all-executions feasibility requirement. The new result does not narrow the interval between the known conditional lower endpoint and two.

The standard linear relaxation has fractional openings \(0\le y_s\le1\), assignments \(0\le x_{c,s}\le y_s\), \(\sum_s x_{c,s}=1\) for every client, and \(\sum_s y_s\le k\), minimizing \(\sum_{c,s}d(c,s)x_{c,s}\). Its integrality gap approaches two. For a unit-edge star with \(q\ge3\) leaves, all vertices as facilities, leaves as clients and \(k=q-1\), the integral optimum is two. A feasible fractional solution has center opening \(1/(q-1)\), each leaf opening \((q-2)/(q-1)\), and each client assigned to its own leaf and the center in those proportions. Its cost is \(q/(q-1)\), yielding a gap at least \(2(q-1)/q\). This is a barrier for that relaxation, not an unconditional computational lower bound against the true integral optimum.

Cohen-Addad–Gupta–Kumar–Lee–Li’s ICALP 2019 Theorem 1 attains \(1+2/e+\varepsilon\) in time \(f(k,\varepsilon)n^{O(1)}\). That fixed-parameter guarantee allows a dependence on \(k\) which need not be polynomial. Here \(k\) is part of the unrestricted input, so the parameterized result does not establish the corresponding polynomial-time factor.
The March 2026 low-dimensional Euclidean work improves approximation-scheme running times by using geometric structure. Its guarantees do not apply to arbitrary metric tables.

The July 2026 spectral dual-fitting preprint improves k-Means guarantees in Euclidean and general metrics. That objective sums squared distances, which changes both approximation and hardness constants; the paper does not give a smaller general k-Median ratio.

The requested approximation must refer to the same input class, randomness convention and facility budget. A fixed-parameter runtime, a relaxation-gap example or a guarantee opening extra facilities does not establish this polynomial-time upper bound.
